name: Peoples of the Southwest (Pueblo, Diné, Apache, O’odham)
summary: The peoples of the American Southwest and north-west Mexico: the Pueblo farmers such as the Hopi and Zuni, the Diné (Navajo) and Apache, and the O’odham; the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove out the Spanish for 12 years.

location.value: Arizona, New Mexico and north-west Mexico.

climate.value: Dry and hot, with cold winters on the plateau.

disasters.value: Droughts and cold spells affected farming.

urbanisation.value: Adobe and stone pueblos, some lived in for 900 years (Acoma, Taos).

disease.value: Smallpox and other diseases killed many after Spanish contact.

migration.value: The Diné (Navajo) and Apache arrived from the north about 1400.

economicBase.value: Irrigated maize farming (Pueblo, O’odham); hunting, raiding and herding (Apache, Diné).

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with the Plains and Mexico (turquoise, macaws).

wealth.value: Turquoise, cotton cloth and, later, sheep were valued goods.

inequality.value: Mostly small-scale societies; some ranked chiefs and families.

governmentType.value: Each pueblo was self-governing. Apache and Diné bands are not covered by these pages.

keyRulers.value: Popé planned and led the Pueblo Revolt. Geronimo surrendered in 1886 with 30 followers. Manuelito is not mentioned.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Pueblo Revolt and Apache Wars (checked 13 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Religious leaders and clan elders held authority.

institutions.value: Kiva societies and councils guided ceremonies and decisions.

stability.value: Long-lasting villages, some of which have been inhabited for centuries.

eliteConflict.value: Local disputes and raids between peoples.

armyAndTech.value: Bows; horses from the Spanish after 1600.

majorWars.value: The Pueblo Revolt (10–21 August 1680) and the Apache Wars (1849–86, with minor fighting to 1924). The Long Walk of the Navajo is mentioned without a date.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Pueblo Revolt and Apache Wars (checked 13 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Reservations were created after the 1860s as the United States took control.

alliancesRivals.value: Relations with the Spanish, Comanche, Mexico and the United States shaped history.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled local technologies.

scienceEducation.value: Calendars based on the sun and expert farming in dry land.

communicationTransport.value: Trails, with horses after the Spanish arrived.

religion.value: Franciscan missionaries tried to replace traditional worship, and Fray Alonso de Posada outlawed Kachina dances.

languageWriting.value: Keresan, Tanoan, Hopi, Zuni, Navajo, Apache, O’odham.

socialStructure.value: Clans, matrilineal in many Pueblo peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: Identity rested on each people, village and language rather than one state.

dailyLife.value: Maize, beans and squash; adobe houses or hogans.

neighbours.value: Plains peoples, Comanche, Spanish New Mexico.

ideasReligions.value: Ceremonial cycles tied to rain and the farming year.

colonisation.value: Spanish colonisation from the 1500s; later Mexico and the United States.

riseSignals.value: The Ancestral Puebloans emerged around the 12th century BCE (Early Basketmaker II) in the Four Corners; population grew fast from 700 to 1130 CE (Pueblo I and II). The page covers only the Ancestral Puebloans, not the Diné, Apache or O’odham.

peakPeriod.value: A “Golden Age” between about 900 and 1150; the largest roads were built with the great houses between 1000 and 1125 CE.

declineSignals.value: Spanish conquest began in 1598, though the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove them out for twelve years.

outcome.value: The Chacoans left the canyon, probably because of climate change starting with a 50-year drought from 1130; a 300-year Great Drought followed and people left their homes in the 12th and 13th centuries. The page does not give a date of about 1300.

overallCertainty.value: Known from archaeology, oral history and Spanish and later records; population figures are estimates.
